why: Comparing two ripple rings crossing in a pan with a shiny card helps your child explain how a hologram records light waves, not a picture.
teaser: Tilt a card with a bird inside, cross two ripples in a pan, then find out why half a hologram still shows the whole thing.
title: How Holograms Work
question: How can a flat, shiny square hold a little bird you can look around?
idea: A hologram is not a picture. It records how two beams of light waves crossed, like two ripple rings crossing in a pan of water. Shine light on that recording, and it bends the light back into the same waves, so your two eyes see depth.

curiosity.intro: Start with a card that hides a bird. Then cross two ripples in a pan, look at what is really on a hologram's film, and break one in half.
curiosity.carryForward: Next time you see a shiny bird or star on a card, tilt it: which way does it turn?

questions.question: What do ripples have to do with light?
questions.notice: Find the tall bumps and the flat calm lines where the two rings cross.
questions.say: Light travels in waves, a bit like ripples. Where two crests meet, they stack into a taller bump. Where a crest meets a dip, they cancel into calm. A hologram records that crossing pattern, made with light instead of water.
questions.try: Put a little water in a baking pan. Tap two fingertips in it at the same time. Look for the calm lines between the bumps.

questions.question: What is really on a hologram's film?
questions.notice: Compare the shell with the fine stripes in the lens. Do they look alike?
questions.say: Not a picture of the shell. A laser beam is split in two. One part bounces off the shell, and one part shines straight on the film. Where they cross, the film records light and dark stripes far thinner than a hair.
questions.try: Look at your fingertip with a magnifying glass. Hologram stripes swirl a bit like that, but they are far tinier and closer together.

questions.question: What happens if a hologram breaks?
questions.notice: Look inside each half. Is any part of the shell missing?
questions.say: Each half still shows the whole shell, just a little blurrier. Light from every spot on the shell landed on every part of the film. It is like peeking through one pane of a window: you still see the whole yard.
questions.try: Look out a window through a paper tube. Move the tube to a different pane. Can you still see the whole tree from each spot?

questions.question: Are floating pictures in movies holograms?
questions.notice: Find the real toy bird below and its reflection in the slanted glass.
questions.say: Usually not. Many stage holograms are an old trick from 1862 called Pepper's ghost. A slanted sheet of clear glass reflects a lit figure, so it seems to float. A real hologram needs film or foil to bend the light.
questions.try: At night, look out a dark window from a bright room. Can you see your room floating outside? That is the same glass trick.

beats.title: A bird inside a card
beats.passage: Little Wonderer tilts a plain card with a shiny square on it. Inside the square, a tiny bird seems to sit behind the card. Tilt it left, and you see one side of the bird. Tilt it right, and you see the other side. Big Wonderer crouches low to look. How can a flat square hold something you can look around?

beats.title: Two ripples cross
beats.passage: Light travels in waves, a little like water. Tap two fingers in a pan of water at once. Two sets of rings spread out and cross. Where two bumps meet, they stack into a taller bump. Where a bump meets a dip, they cancel into a calm line. This crossing is called interference. A hologram records it with light.
beats.prompt: What happens where a bump meets a dip?

foldable.heading: Two ripples cross
foldable.body: Two ripple rings cross in a pan. Bumps stack up, and a bump plus a dip cancels to calm.

beats.title: Stripes, not a picture
beats.passage: To make a hologram, a scientist splits one laser beam into two. One beam bounces off a seashell and onto the film. The other beam shines straight onto the film. The two beams cross, just like the two ripples. The film records bright and dark stripes, finer than a hair. It looks nothing like a shell!
beats.prompt: Why does the film not look like a shell?

foldable.heading: Stripes, not a picture
foldable.body: A laser beam splits in two. Where the beams cross on the film, it records stripes, not a picture.

beats.title: Two halves, both whole
beats.passage: Here is a strange clue. Break a hologram plate in half, and each half still shows the whole shell! Light from every spot on the shell reached every part of the film. So every part holds the whole scene, seen from its own spot. The name hologram comes from Greek words for whole and writing.
beats.prompt: Why does each half still show the whole shell?

foldable.heading: Two halves, both whole
foldable.body: Break a hologram in half. Each half still shows the whole shell, because every spot saw it all.

beats.title: A rainbow bird
beats.passage: Back at the table, the card stands under a lamp. Big Wonderer watches rainbow colors slide across it. The little one points at the bird. Now the guess changes. The bird is not painted on. The shiny foil is stamped with tiny grooves. They bend the lamplight back into the bird's light waves. Each eye gets a slightly different view, so the bird looks deep.
beats.prompt: How do the grooves make the bird look deep?

foldable.heading: A rainbow bird
foldable.body: The bird is not painted. Tiny grooves bend light back into the bird, so each eye sees it a new way.

beats.title: A bird that floats?
beats.passage: In movies, glowing pictures float in the air. Most stage versions are an old trick from 1862. A slanted sheet of clear glass reflects a lit figure, so it seems to hang in the air. A real hologram needs film or foil to bend the light. It also needs a very still table, because one wiggle can blur the stripes. Could light ever draw a bird in empty air?
beats.prompt: What do floating stage pictures use instead of a hologram?

foldable.body: Most floating stage pictures are a reflection in slanted glass. Could light ever draw in empty air?

poem.title: The Bird Who Lives in a Card
lines: Little Wonderer found a small bird in a card,
not painted, not printed, not stuck on too hard.
Tip it this way, and you'll see its left wing.
Tip it that way, and its right! What a thing!
“It’s ripples,” the big one said, filling a pan.
“Tap twice in the water as fast as you can.
Where bumps meet with bumps, they jump up with glee;
where bumps meet with dips, they go flat as can be.”
The film doesn’t hold any bird, any beak,
just stripes upon stripes far too tiny to peek.
Snap it in two, and here’s what you’ll find:
each half keeps the whole bird. (The bird doesn’t mind.)
So Big Wonderer whispered, “Stand still as a stone,
for one wiggle will smudge every stripe that we own.”
The little one froze, not a sneeze, not a sound,
and a bird made of light turned slowly around.
